orders.explanation: Transcript 1 is more capable because it methodically reproduces the bug, identifies the exact root cause (unique constraints being introspected as indexes), applies a minimal and correct fix (`unique=False` when deleting `index_together`), and then adds a targeted regression test that demonstrably fails before the patch and passes after. It also validates the fix across relevant test suites and with an end-to-end migration scenario. Transcript 2 reaches the same core fix but has several dead ends/misuses of migration state APIs, doesn’t add a regression test to the suite, and provides less comprehensive verification.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only identifies and applies the minimal, correct fix (`unique=False` when deleting `index_together`), but also adds a targeted regression test that demonstrably fails without the patch and passes with it. It validates behavior via reproductions, runs relevant test suites (schema and migrations), and even checks an end-to-end makemigrations/migrate scenario. Transcript 1 eventually finds the right fix and reproduces the bug, but it has more dead ends and doesn’t complete the same level of testing and integration verification.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it efficiently located the exact upstream Django commit that fixed the issue, inspected its full diff, and then applied a byte-for-byte matching source change. It also validated behavior against the newly added upstream tests (by temporarily checking out the test changes) and confirmed the failure mode without the fix, demonstrating stronger repo navigation and provenance-checking. Despite some minor missteps in test invocation and ad-hoc reproduction setup, it ultimately converged on the canonical fix with solid verification.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it quickly identified the exact upstream Django commit that fixes the issue, reproduced its diff precisely, and validated behavior by showing the new test fails without the patch and passes with it. It also managed the test runner correctly (including resolving label/settings issues), ran broader regression tests, and ensured the final working tree contained only the intended source change to avoid conflicts with the harness-applied tests. Transcript 2 arrives at a correct fix, but it relies on ad‑hoc simulated test edits and is less precise about matching upstream changes and workflow cleanliness.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it not only identifies and fixes the root cause but also adds targeted regression tests in both `tests/test_util_inspect.py` and `tests/test_domain_py.py`, updates `CHANGES`, and performs an end-to-end HTML build verification. It also does broader sanity checking (edge cases, related suites) and cleanly confirms an unrelated pre-existing test failure by stashing/retesting. Transcript 2 reaches a correct code fix and does some verification, but it doesn’t add regression tests or a changelog entry and shows more incidental confusion/missteps (e.g., incorrect test invocation, messy comparisons).

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only identifies and fixes the root cause in `signature_from_str()`, but also adds targeted regression tests at both the util level and the Python-domain rendering level, plus a CHANGES entry. That demonstrates stronger end-to-end engineering judgment (preventing recurrence) and better alignment with typical upstream contribution standards. Transcript 1 implements a solid fix and validates it thoroughly, but omits adding regression coverage.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it correctly identified the exact upstream Sphinx PR/commit that implemented the feature, applied the full patch (including the crucial `merge_members_option()` behavior, updated option parsing, filtering semantics, docs, and deprecation notes), and validated it with targeted tests while recognizing unrelated pre-existing test failures. Transcript 2 made an incomplete/incorrect local modification: it changed the option type and some filtering logic but omitted the necessary merge behavior, introduced documentation/CHANGES inaccuracies, and spent significant effort debugging self-created tests rather than ensuring the core integration matched Sphinx’s established design.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it efficiently locates the exact upstream fix commit (via `git log --grep`), inspects the authoritative diff, and applies it cleanly and comprehensively across code, docs, and changelog. It also validates behavior with targeted tests and checks that remaining failures are pre-existing environment issues, demonstrating strong debugging discipline. Transcript 1 implements a partial/manual patch, creates noisy temporary tests, and gets derailed by avoidable assertion/import/test-target issues, indicating weaker strategy and execution.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it quickly isolates the exact faulty parsing logic, applies the minimal correct fix (`split` → `rsplit` on the param “type name” form), and validates it with a tight reproduction. Transcript 1 eventually finds the same fix but takes a much more circuitous route, introduces unrelated repository modifications (setup.py/tox.ini) into the working diff, and ends with test failures and extra noise that a stronger model would avoid or cleanly separate. Overall, Transcript 2 demonstrates better focus, patch hygiene, and signal-to-noise.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only reproduces and diagnoses the bug correctly, but also locates the exact upstream fixing commit in the repository history, applies the minimal correct change (`split` → `rsplit`), and validates behavior against the relevant regression test logic. It additionally runs multiple targeted test suites and checks that unrelated failures are pre-existing, demonstrating stronger end-to-end engineering rigor than Transcript 1, which stops after the fix and a partial/unfinished test run without adding or referencing a corresponding regression test or changelog entry.

Transcript 1 is markedly more capable: it delivers a clean, modular ARS implementation that matches the required `ars(density_function, domain, n = sample_count)` interface, performs log‑concavity checks correctly, and includes a comprehensive, well-structured test suite with clear PASS/FAIL reporting; it also robustly handles vectorization fallback and writes the required sample files. Transcript 2 shows repeated conceptual and implementation errors (e.g., incorrect squeeze, missing acceptance test for a time, numerical issues, and a stricter `n` validation that incorrectly rejects `n=0`), plus side effects on sourcing; although it eventually converges, the process and final behavior are less reliable and less aligned with the spec.

Transcript 1 shows substantially deeper algorithmic understanding and engineering rigor: it iteratively diagnoses and fixes multiple subtle ARS failure modes (incorrect squeeze, missing acceptance test, numerical underflow, parallel-tangent intersections, non-monotone hull boundaries, domain-grid infinities) and ends with a robust implementation plus an extensive, clearly reported test suite and stress testing. Transcript 2 produces a cleaner-looking solution but initially contains a serious concavity-check bug (sorting `x` and `dh` independently) and its numerical/stability handling and validation (e.g., NA treated as zero density) is less thorough overall. The breadth of edge-case coverage and numerically stable hull construction in Transcript 1 indicates the more capable model.

Transcript 1 shows stronger end-to-end competence: it correctly derives the 6-edge skeleton via properly implemented partial-correlation CI tests, applies the identifiability/tiebreak rule appropriately, and fits/samples a coherent linear-Gaussian SEM while writing all required artifacts directly to the specified paths. Transcript 2 ultimately succeeds and leverages pgmpy effectively, but it contains multiple substantive missteps (incorrect partial-correlation implementation, several API confusions, and validation indexing bugs) that required repeated debugging and backtracking. The cleaner, more reliably correct workflow in Transcript 1 indicates the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it robustly navigates the constrained environment (no Python initially), installs the needed tooling, correctly identifies the 6-edge skeleton via conditional-independence/partial-correlation checks, and then uses an appropriate Bayesian-network implementation (pgmpy LinearGaussianBayesianNetwork) to fit parameters, apply an explicit do-intervention, and sample. It also performs extensive verification of file formats, edge sets, and post-intervention distributional properties, catching and fixing multiple validation-script bugs along the way. Transcript 2 is mostly correct but contains weaker methodological rigor and some inconsistent claims (e.g., about CI p-values and covariance reconstruction error), and relies on a hand-rolled SEM sampler rather than a BN package with intervention semantics.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger debugging and systems reasoning: it isolates the crash to libstdc++’s patched facet-registration teardown, confirms the exact runtime trigger with GDB, and iterates when the first proposed “use_facet in user_init” approach is optimized away under -O2. It then produces a robust fix that forces the registration via a library-defined code path (floating formatting through iostreams) with an observable result to prevent dead-code elimination, avoiding reliance on calling a nonstandard `std::_Facet_Register_impl` symbol. Transcript 2 reaches a working fix too, but it relies on declaring and calling an internal libstdc++ function in `namespace std` (more brittle/less standard) and contains more dead-end investigation artifacts.

Transcript 1 shows stronger end-to-end debugging skill: it precisely isolates the failure to the custom libstdc++ facet tidy destructor, proves the allocation/free ordering issue with gdb/nm/objdump, and implements the most direct and robust fix by explicitly invoking `std::_Facet_Register_impl()` at the safe time (`user_init`). Transcript 2 also reaches a correct fix, but only after an initial ineffective approach (facet warmup via `use_facet` that didn’t trigger the library path) and a longer detour reasoning about header/library instantiation. The first transcript’s fix is simpler, more targeted, and better justified/validated.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a markedly stronger cryptanalytic understanding: it identifies a probability‑1 differential in the round function, derives an exact last‑round key constraint, and reduces the 16‑bit key[5] seed space with just a handful of chosen pairs—yielding a clean, fast, dependency‑free implementation. Transcript 2 spends substantial time on exploratory/empirical characteristics, makes a key mistake in the chosen difference, and even relies on installing/using NumPy (with a later fallback), producing a more complex and less principled solution path. The directness, correctness-by-design (not just by testing), and simplicity of Transcript 1 indicate the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it identifies and proves a probability‑1 differential through the round function and then derives a clean, deterministic constraint on the last-round subkey, yielding a very simple and fast key‑recovery procedure. Transcript 1 eventually succeeds but relies on extensive trial‑and‑error exploration, an initially incorrect differential setup, and heavier scoring machinery (including an optional numpy path and a slower fallback), reflecting less direct understanding of the cipher’s exploitable structure. Transcript 2’s solution is both more elegant and more robustly justified with fewer moving parts.

Transcript 1 is clearly more capable: it derives a correct meet-in-the-middle strategy quickly, implements a tight C attack that runs in ~0.5s, recovers both seeds and expanded round keys, and performs clean end-to-end verification (including re-encrypt checks) with minimal thrashing. Transcript 2 eventually reaches the same key, but only after multiple incorrect equations, several broken/segfaulting C implementations, extensive ad‑hoc debugging, and a much more convoluted workflow. The efficiency, correctness on the first serious implementation, and clarity of the cryptanalytic reasoning in Transcript 1 indicate the stronger model.

Transcript 2 is markedly more capable: it derives a correct meet-in-the-middle relation, implements an efficient C attack that runs in ~0.5s, cleanly recovers seeds/round keys, and verifies correctness by checking all pairs and re-encrypting the recovered plaintexts. Transcript 1 contains substantial thrashing—incorrect equations, failed/buggy C implementation, long debugging detours (including confusion about the binaries), and only later arrives at the correct optimized approach. The clarity, correctness, and engineering efficiency of Transcript 2 indicate the stronger model.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it immediately identifies the root cause via `git diff`, ties it directly to the failing test, and applies the minimal, correct fix to `_hkey`/`_hval` to raise `ValueError` for CR/LF/NUL. It also produces a `report.jsonl` entry using the expected CWE ID formatting (`"cwe-93"`), whereas Transcript 1 writes `"CWE-93"` (likely failing the “exact CWE-ids” constraint) and includes extra missteps (cookie check confusion, unnecessary revert cycle) that indicate weaker precision.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it follows the task requirements more precisely and consistently: it correctly identifies the CRLF/header injection issue, restores the missing validation in `_hkey`/`_hval`, and writes `report.jsonl` using the required CWE ID formatting (`"cwe-93"` matching the prompt’s example). Transcript 2 has notable inconsistencies (it reports `["CWE-93"]` with different casing than required, and it later “fixes” by checking out `bottle.py` from `HEAD`, which undermines the earlier vulnerability narrative and makes the workflow less reliable). Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates clearer diagnosis-to-fix-to-test closure aligned with the instructions.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it executes a clean, direct setup with minimal detours: it configures SSH password auth, creates the bare repo, writes a correct post-receive hook, configures Nginx+TLS, and validates the full grading flow without stumbling. Transcript 2 eventually reaches a working state, but shows more trial-and-error (Nginx port conflict, an initial failed dev commit due to missing git identity) and introduces unnecessary/unsafe config (e.g., `PermitRootLogin yes`). Transcript 1 is therefore more reliable and production-appropriate given the same task constraints.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger operational awareness and robustness: it detects and resolves an existing Nginx port/name conflict, adapts to the environment’s pre-provisioned default site/cert, and uses a safer deployment strategy (`git archive` + clean target directory) that avoids leaving stale/untracked files in the webroot. It also performs comprehensive end-to-end verification (including timing) and then re-initializes the bare repo to a truly pristine state, reducing grading-harness flakiness. Transcript 2 works for the tested case, but its `checkout -f` deployment can leave stale files and is less robust overall, and it makes more assumptions about Nginx layout by removing the default site rather than reconciling conflicts.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger engineering capability: it identifies a faster LAPACK path, benchmarks alternatives, handles complex eigenvector reconstruction correctly, and ultimately builds a working CPython extension with robust correctness checks and consistent speedups over the NumPy reference. Transcript 2 attempts a Numba-based custom QR approach but repeatedly hits algorithmic bugs, nondeterminism, import-time failures, and ends with worse-than-reference performance, indicating weaker implementation skill and incomplete delivery.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially stronger problem-solving and engineering ability: it identifies the key performance bottleneck (NumPy eig overhead), benchmarks alternatives, then implements and iteratively hardens a fast solution using LAPACK via a compiled extension, including careful handling of complex eigenvectors, overflow-safe residual checks, and robust fallbacks. It also validates speedups with repeated timing and broad correctness sweeps and ends with a viable integration into `/app/eigen.py`. Transcript 1, by contrast, spends extensive effort on a custom QR/Hessenberg approach with many correctness bugs, nondeterminism, and ultimately does not produce a stable faster-than-NumPy implementation.

Transcript 1 is more capable: it identifies key cost-model invariants early (S_max/G_max derived from real requests, declared shape only impacts compile cost), then builds a principled DP partitioner per aligned-prompt group and adds a targeted “surgical” step to control p95 inflation—yielding comfortably passing metrics with only 2 shapes. It also demonstrates stronger debugging discipline and validation (coverage, per-batch shape consistency, global shape cap) with fewer dead-ends. Transcript 2 eventually succeeds but takes a more error-prone, ad‑hoc path (multiple incorrect/slow solver attempts, fragile heuristics, and thin margins before retuning), indicating comparatively weaker execution and reasoning.

Transcript 1 shows a stronger grasp of the cost model’s key levers (notably that runtime S_max/G_max come from the actual batch contents and that declared shapes mainly affect compile cost), then exploits this with a principled “dominance-preserving” merge strategy that reduces sequential time while tightly controlling pad/p95/cost. It also includes more robust end-to-end validation and an explicit batch-ordering trick to minimize the compile-latency hit. Transcript 2 eventually succeeds but involves more trial-and-error, several implementation missteps/patches, and a more convoluted optimization path before converging.

Transcript 1 shows stronger operational competence: it quickly identifies the Mailman→Postfix LMTP integration path, leverages Mailman’s auto-generated Postfix hash maps (`postfix_lmtp`, `postfix_domains`), and configures Postfix with standard, minimal settings that satisfy confirmation-address handling via `recipient_delimiter=+`. It also validates each flow and achieves a clean, stable `eval.py` pass with fewer missteps and less ad‑hoc patching. Transcript 2 eventually works but takes a more error-prone route (regexp maps, empty-result local_recipient_maps bug, chroot-related recipient failures) and requires multiple reactive fixes and extra cleanup, indicating comparatively weaker initial design choices.

Transcript 1 shows substantially stronger operational troubleshooting and systems understanding: it identifies and fixes multiple real-world integration pitfalls (Postfix smtpd chroot preventing passwd/map lookups, regexp map “empty string” causing 451 errors, Mailman list directory ownership issues after creating lists as root, and correct enum setting for policies). It validates behavior end-to-end with the provided eval and additional targeted tests, then leaves the system in a clean, reproducible state with correct running users and ports. Transcript 2 also succeeds, but it relies on a simpler/less robust approach (running Mailman as root and using hash local_recipient_maps assumptions) and does less deep debugging and hardening.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger problem-solving and robustness: it infers the mapping by searching for the smallest consistent periodic rule (trying multiple indexings and periods) rather than hard-coding a specific `% 3` pattern from the visible examples. It also handles repository hygiene better (removing the `.DS_Store` artifact, keeping the merge result clean) and provides clearer verification of the merge commit structure and exact element-wise correctness. Transcript 2 reaches a working solution for the shown examples, but its implementation is narrower (assumes period 3) and it leaves extraneous files committed.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only completes the git-branch/bundle/merge workflow correctly, but also produces a cleaner, more disciplined merged repository state (notably removing the `.DS_Store` artifact rather than committing it). Its `map` implementation is more robustly inferred from the observed non-zero constraints (searching for the smallest consistent period and indexing scheme) while still meeting the required interface and passing the provided examples. Transcript 1 is thorough and tests heavily, but it leaves extraneous files in the final tree and hard-codes a narrower rule with ad hoc fallback behavior.

Transcript 1 delivers a clean, end-to-end solution without missteps: it generates the key and cert with the specified subject fields, sets correct permissions (including securing the combined PEM), produces the requested verification artifacts, and provides a Python verifier that works in the given environment without relying on private/unstable Python APIs. Transcript 2 ultimately succeeds, but it initially ships a broken Python script (wrong subject parsing), then patches it, and it depends on `ssl._ssl._test_decode_cert`, a private interface that is less robust across Python versions. Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger reliability and execution.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger problem-solving and technical depth: when the initial Python parsing failed due to the subject tuple structure, it investigated the actual data shape, corrected the iteration logic, and then further refined the script to eliminate a deprecation warning. It also proactively added a SAN extension (important for modern TLS) and performed thorough cryptographic validation (modulus match, self-verify) beyond the minimum. Transcript 2 is solid and pragmatic, but its CN extraction relies on brittle string parsing of OpenSSL output and avoids proper certificate parsing, indicating slightly less robustness.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it delivers a robust polyglot that is correct for large \(N\) in both languages, implementing arbitrary-precision Fibonacci in C to match Python’s unbounded integers. It also refines the polyglot structure to eliminate compiler warnings and validates correctness extensively (including cross-checking with an independent big-integer implementation). Transcript 2 ultimately relies on 64-bit `long long` in C and visibly overflows at \(N=93\), so it does not truly satisfy “print the kth Fibonacci number” for general \(N\) even though Python does.

Transcript 2 demonstrates higher capability by delivering a more robust solution: it implements arbitrary-precision Fibonacci on the C side so the polyglot computes the correct kth Fibonacci number for large N without overflow, matching Python’s unbounded integers. It also converges on a cleaner, warning-free polyglot structure (`#if 0` + balanced `''''` plus a C block comment with `#*/`) and performs extensive independent correctness checks on large inputs. Transcript 1 eventually produces a working polyglot, but its C implementation is limited to `long long` (overflowing at f(93)) and the development path includes a more fragile quoting approach that temporarily broke Python execution.

Transcript 1 is markedly more capable: it quickly identifies the key constraint (need `console=ttyS0` over a telnet-backed serial), extracts the kernel/initramfs robustly without privileged mounts, starts QEMU daemonized with the correct serial telnet chardev, and blocks until the login prompt is actually observed on port 6665. Transcript 2 is extremely inefficient and error-prone, repeatedly breaks its own tooling, over-engineers an initrd patching scheme, and spends large effort debugging self-inflicted issues before reaching a working state. Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger planning, execution, and minimal-correctness engineering.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it discovered (and empirically verified) the key failure mode: QEMU’s `-serial telnet:...` drops guest output when no client is connected, so a normal boot-time getty prompt will often not be visible on a later telnet connection. It then engineered and validated a robust fix (patching the initramfs to install an inittab-respawned daemon that reprints the login prompt when idle), and implemented a true “block until ready” signal. Transcript 2 is competent but relies on “press Enter once” to redraw the prompt, which does not fully satisfy the requirement that the user will immediately see the login prompt upon connecting.

Transcript 1 shows stronger problem-solving rigor: it iteratively refines the pattern, builds extensive targeted tests plus fuzzing/oracle checks, and validates tricky boundary conditions and IPv4 constraints (including guarding against matching an IP that’s merely a substring of a longer dotted numeric sequence). It also ensures exactly one capturing group so `re.findall` returns only the date, and demonstrates the regex works under multiline scanning semantics. Transcript 2 eventually arrives at a correct regex, but spends substantial effort on a Perl harness quirk and does less substantive refinement of the actual matching edge cases than Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 shows substantially stronger problem-solving and engineering rigor: it decomposes the requirements, builds a carefully validated date/IP pattern, ensures “last date on the line” via greedy matching, and systematically tests many edge cases. It also adapts to the environment constraints (no Python available) by constructing equivalent Perl-based validation and debugging multiple toolchain quirks until the final regex file is verified. Transcript 2 is competent, but its development is more ad hoc and includes several midstream revisions and tooling breakages; overall it demonstrates less robust reasoning and debugging depth than Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it builds a fully self-describing, constraint-guaranteed shard format (tar.gz shards) with strong safety and correctness features: adaptive packing to ensure the 15MB limit, automatic directory-depth selection to enforce ≤30 entries per directory, manifest splitting/compression if it grows too large, and path-safety checks during restore. It also restores substantially more metadata precisely (including nanosecond mtimes via PAX headers and symlink mtimes) and rigorously tests many edge cases. Transcript 2 is simpler and works on the sample, but it hard-fails if the manifest exceeds 15MB (no splitting), relies on a fixed manifest filename, and is generally less robust/scalable despite passing its tests.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it implements a simpler, more formally correct reversible format: fixed-size chunk files (≤15 MiB) plus a manifest, with deterministic balanced fan-out ensuring the ≤30-entries-per-directory constraint by construction. It also verifies integrity on restore via per-file SHA-256 and performs an atomic in-place swap, and it thoroughly tests many edge cases (symlinks, empty dirs, big files, depth-3 trees) without needing iterative bug-fixing. Transcript 2 eventually works, but it relies on complex tar.gz packing heuristics, initially misses key requirements (dir-symlinks, nanosecond mtimes), and lacks end-to-end integrity verification beyond size/MD5 checks in testing.

Transcript 2 demonstrates stronger end-to-end competence: it not only ports the Stan code and matches sampling hyperparameters, but also validates the precise RStan→Stan services mapping by inspecting RStan’s R/C++ sources (e.g., how `iter/warmup` become `num_samples/num_warmup`, how `init_r` maps to `init_radius`, and how `seed` and `chain_id` interact via `create_rng`). It also performs targeted smoke tests to confirm the PyStan/httpstan wrapper accepts the intended kwargs and that draw shapes match expectations. Transcript 1 is solid and even adds a memory optimization, but Transcript 2 is more rigorous about exact sampling equivalence and reproducibility details.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger technical competence by deeply validating PyStan 3/httpstan parameter mappings against RStan (including confirming chain/seed behavior and iter→num_samples semantics via RStan source inspection), handling environment constraints correctly (PEP 668, import name `stan`), and explicitly matching all sampling hyperparameters (including defaults like stepsize). Transcript 2 is broadly correct, but is less rigorous about exact equivalence details (e.g., relies on defaults more, has a brittle `np.loadtxt` dimensionality check, and ends with a failed scalar assertion), indicating slightly weaker robustness and verification discipline.

Transcript 1 is more capable. It anticipates and solves real deployment constraints (CPU-only, cgroup CPU quota/oversubscription, memory scaling via cropped masks, deterministic overlap arbitration using logits/distance transforms, and OpenCV compatibility) while staying within the allowed Python packages and avoiding system-level dependencies. Transcript 2 is much more ad‑hoc (multiple patch cycles, initial reliance on apt-get/system libs, attempted SciPy use, and a more brittle overlap/polygonization pipeline), making it less robust for a hidden test environment.

Transcript 1 demonstrates markedly stronger engineering and evaluation: it iteratively prototypes prompting strategies, optimizes CPU performance (thread tuning), handles CSV index/no-index cases, implements overlap removal with an efficient owner-map, and adds multiple robust post-processing safeguards (largest CC, polygonization fallback, non-rectangle guarantees, and repeated overlap checks) with extensive validation and determinism checks. Transcript 2 is solid and includes a clever overlap arbitration scheme, but it shows more mid-development instability (multiple rewrites, performance surprises, and a less comprehensive set of robustness measures around CSV fidelity and polygon validity). Overall, Transcript 1 exhibits deeper debugging, more rigorous verification, and a more defensive final pipeline.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it not only derives a correct query, but also diagnoses and fixes a real SPARQL-engine compatibility issue (rdflib’s inability to parse subqueries inside `FILTER EXISTS`) by restructuring the query into a standard SPARQL 1.1 form. It additionally validates the final query across two different engines (rdflib and Jena), demonstrating stronger debugging skill, standards awareness, and robustness checking than Transcript 1, which only validates in rdflib.

Transcript 1 shows stronger capability through deeper tool-driven debugging and adaptability: it identifies an rdflib parser limitation (subquery inside `FILTER EXISTS`), restructures the query to be standards-compliant across engines, and validates results with multiple SPARQL implementations. It also demonstrates robust environment problem-solving (installing dependencies, testing counts, and verifying query outputs), whereas Transcript 2 mainly validates within rdflib and does not address cross-engine quirks. Overall, Transcript 1 exhibits more sophisticated troubleshooting and portability awareness.

Transcript 2 is more capable. It completes the task with a simpler, more standard workflow (configure → make → make install), ensuring `sqlite3` is on `PATH` via installation rather than a symlink. It also performs stronger end-to-end verification of coverage by checking for `__gcov` symbols, confirming `.gcda` generation, and running `gcov` on the correct `.gcno` file to obtain non-zero executed-line coverage, whereas Transcript 1’s `gcov` check is partially inconsistent (0%/missing data due to targeting the wrong file).

Transcript 1 is more capable because it performs a clean, standard build-and-install workflow (`./configure` with coverage flags, `make`, `make install`) that truly “makes it available in PATH” via installation to `/usr/local/bin`, and it verifies end-to-end that runtime execution generates `.gcda` files and that `gcov` can correctly process the produced data (after correcting an initial file-choice mismatch). Transcript 2 is less robust: it relies on a symlink rather than installing, does some confusing redundant extraction/moves, and its `gcov sqlite3.c` check misleadingly reports 0% due to using the wrong data file (without a follow-up confirming nonzero coverage from the right `.gcno/.gcda` pair).
